analysis.one_liner: Bars internet providers from blocking, slowing, or charging extra for lawful online content.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on May 8, 2008 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written 'net neutrality' rules into the antitrust laws. It barred broadband providers like cable and phone companies from blocking or slowing lawful websites, from charging websites extra fees to reach customers at full speed, from banning the devices of their choice, and from hiding the real terms of service. It also required equal treatment of competing data streams and required providers to disclose their practices clearly. The bill never moved past its initial referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday internet users, small websites, startups, and any business or person who publishes or sells online. The bill guaranteed them access to the full internet at equal speed, without paying providers' tolls or being outcompeted by services the provider owns or favors.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibited broadband providers from blocking, impairing, or discriminating against any person's access to lawful content, applications, or services, and from charging an extra fee to escape that treatment [S2] [S3].

Required providers to offer their own services to others on the same reasonable, nondiscriminatory terms they give their own affiliates, and to interconnect with other providers on those terms [S2] [S3].
Barred providers from banning devices that do not damage or degrade the network, protecting consumers' ability to use the hardware of their choice [S2] [S3].
Required clear, plain-language disclosure of any terms, conditions, or limits on service, so customers know what they are buying [S2] [S3].

Allowed reasonable network management, emergency communications priority, law enforcement compliance, and consumer-protection tools, so the rules did not stop providers from running their networks [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers — cable and telephone companies — would lose the ability to collect paid-prioritization fees from websites and services, and would face antitrust lawsuits for discriminatory practices.

drawbacks.text: By routing the rules through the Clayton Act, violations would be enforced mainly through private antitrust lawsuits, a slower and less predictable path than direct FCC regulation, and one that favors parties able to fund litigation [S3].

Broadband providers argued that bans on charging content companies for faster delivery remove a revenue stream they said helped fund network investment, and that they need flexibility to manage congestion — the bill answered this by allowing reasonable, nondiscriminatory network management, but the investment objection was the core industry case against any net neutrality mandate [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For internet users and small online businesses the protections were substantial and directly valuable: equal access to the whole internet without tolls. The main real cost falls on broadband providers, who would lose paid-prioritization revenue; the design tradeoff is enforcement through antitrust litigation rather than a regulator, which makes the rules harder to invoke for ordinary people who cannot afford to sue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no vote, nothing — before that Congress expired in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the bill on May 8, 2008, with Rep. Zoe Lofgren as cosponsor [S1] [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers kept their freedom to block, slow, or charge for prioritized internet access without legal consequence, since no comparable federal net neutrality statute was enacted in that Congress.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers, Jr.
for.role: Sponsor; Chair of the House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee, which he chaired; the committee took no further action on it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by the bill's sponsor
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Cable and telephone broadband industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed net neutrality legislation in this era, arguing paid prioritization and network-management flexibility were needed to fund and operate their networks.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats were attached to the bill and it never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists to show how the parties lined up.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from blocking or slowing rivals' content, from charging websites extra for fast lanes, and from restricting customers' devices — eliminating a growing fee stream built on controlling what customers can reach.

industries.industry: Internet content, application, and service companies (especially small sites and startups)
industries.note: The bill guaranteed equal-speed access to users without paying providers' tolls, lowering the barrier for small and new online businesses to reach an audience.
Consumers would get a guaranteed open internet and plain-language disclosure of service terms, protecting them from hidden throttling and device restrictions.
